sections.h: Third Isaiah: chapters 56–66
sections.b: Since Bernhard Duhm (1892), many scholars have called Isaiah 56–66 "Third Isaiah" (Trito-Isaiah): prophecies from Judah after the return from Babylon, when the temple was being rebuilt or had been, and the community was poor and divided. Some think of one prophet, others of a circle of disciples who read and extended chapters 40–55. The chapters are arranged around a center: the vision of Zion's light and the anointed speaker in chapters 60–62, framed by the warrior who arms himself (Isaiah 59:15–20) and returns from Edom (Isaiah 63:1–6), and on the outside by the welcome of foreigners (Isaiah 56:1–8) and the gathering of the nations (Isaiah 66:18–24). Many readers see chapters 65–66 as written to close the whole book, echoing chapter 1. Traditional readers, Jewish and Christian, have held that Isaiah himself saw this future. Either way, the chapters speak to people who had come home and found the promises not yet fulfilled.
sections.refs: Isaiah 56:1–8; Isaiah 59:15–20; Isaiah 60:1–3; Isaiah 61:1–3; Isaiah 63:1–6; Isaiah 66:18–24; Isaiah 1:1

sections.h: Isaiah 56 and 66: foreigners at God's altar
sections.b: Isaiah 56:1–8 is the Bible's strongest welcome to outsiders. The foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD must not say, "The LORD is sure to separate me from his people", and eunuchs, who were barred from the assembly in Deuteronomy 23:1, are promised "a marker and a name that is better than sons and daughters" (Isaiah 56:5). Foreigners who keep the Sabbath and hold to the covenant will bring offerings to God's altar, "for my house will be called a house of prayer for all the peoples" (Isaiah 56:7), words Jesus quoted when he cleared the temple (Mark 11:17). The book ends the same way: God sends messengers to the nations and takes "some of them too to be Levite priests" (Isaiah 66:21). The passage stands in tension with the separation from foreigners in Ezra 9–10 and Nehemiah 13:1–3, and scholars still debate whether it answers them.
sections.refs: Isaiah 56:1–8; Isaiah 66:18–21; Deuteronomy 23:1–8; Nehemiah 13:1–3; Ezra 9:1–2; Mark 11:17; Acts 8:26–39

sections.h: Isaiah 56 and 58: the Sabbath as a sign and a delight
sections.b: Isaiah 56–58 gives the Sabbath a central place. Keeping it is the mark of foreigners and eunuchs who belong to the LORD (Isaiah 56:2, 4, 6). Isaiah 58:13–14 then calls it "a delight, the LORD's holy day honored": a day for turning away from "your own business" and taking delight in the LORD, with the promise that God will set his people "riding over the land's high places". The rabbis drew from these verses the duty of oneg Shabbat, delight in the Sabbath with good food, clothes and rest, and the rule against talking business on the day (Bavli Shabbat 113a–b). The book's last vision has "all flesh" coming to worship "from Sabbath to Sabbath" (Isaiah 66:23). Christians differ on how the promise applies to them: see the traditions card on Isaiah 58.
sections.refs: Isaiah 56:2–7; Isaiah 58:13–14; Isaiah 66:23; Exodus 20:8–11; Exodus 31:13

sections.h: Isaiah 58: the fast God chooses
sections.b: Isaiah 58 answers a complaint: "Why did we fast, and you did not see?" (Isaiah 58:3). God replies that the people fast while they drive their workers hard and quarrel. The fast he chooses is "to unlock the fetters of wickedness, to loosen the ropes of the yoke, to send the crushed away free", to share bread with the hungry and "take the afflicted and the uprooted under a roof" (Isaiah 58:6–7). The chapter is the prophetic reading (haftarah) on the morning of Yom Kippur, the great fast day of the Jewish year, so that every year the fast is interpreted by its demand for justice. Christians have read it in Lent, and the early church writers Barnabas and Hermas used it to define true fasting.
sections.refs: Isaiah 58:1–12; Leviticus 16:29–31; Zechariah 7:3–10; Matthew 6:16–18

sections.h: "My servants" in Isaiah 56–66
sections.b: After Isaiah 53 the servant of the LORD is no longer one figure: from Isaiah 54:17 on the word is plural, and in chapters 56–66 it is always plural: foreigners may become God's servants (Isaiah 56:6), the people pray "for the sake of your servants" (Isaiah 63:17), and chapters 65–66 set "my servants", who eat, drink and rejoice, against "you who abandon the LORD" (Isaiah 65:11–15). Many scholars think the servants are the faithful heirs of the servant of chapters 40–55, a group who trembled at God's word and were pushed out by their own brothers (Isaiah 66:5). The anointed speaker of Isaiah 61:1–3, who claims the Spirit and a mission to the humble, is often read as continuing the servant's work, and Jesus took up that text in Luke 4:18–21.
sections.refs: Isaiah 54:17; Isaiah 56:6; Isaiah 61:1–3; Isaiah 63:17; Isaiah 65:8–15; Isaiah 66:5; Isaiah 66:14; Luke 4:18–21

sections.h: Isaiah 61: the year of release
sections.b: Isaiah 61:1–2 uses the jubilee's own word, deror, "release" (Leviticus 25:10), when the anointed speaker is sent "to proclaim release to the captives" and "a year of the LORD's goodwill". Isaiah 58:6 has a similar call to "send the crushed away free". The jubilee becomes a picture of God's coming rescue: debts cancelled, slaves freed, land restored. At Qumran, 11QMelchizedek read Isaiah 61 together with Leviticus 25 of a final jubilee, when a heavenly deliverer would proclaim release. In Luke 4:16–21 Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1–2 (with a line from Isaiah 58:6) in the synagogue at Nazareth and says that today the scripture is fulfilled, stopping before "a day of our God's vengeance".
sections.refs: Isaiah 61:1–2; Isaiah 58:6; Leviticus 25:8–13; Jeremiah 34:8–17; Luke 4:16–21

sections.h: Isaiah 61:1: anointed with the Spirit
sections.b: In Isaiah 61:1 an unnamed speaker says, "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the humble". Here the anointing is not with oil for a king or priest, but with the Spirit for a mission of speech: good news, release, comfort. The Targum takes the speaker as the prophet; Christian readers, following Luke 4:18–21 and Acts 10:38 ("It is about Jesus from Nazareth: how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power"), have heard in it the meaning of the title Christ, "the anointed one". The verse joins two ideas that Isaiah keeps together elsewhere: the Spirit resting on the coming king (Isaiah 11:2) and on the servant (Isaiah 42:1).
sections.refs: Isaiah 61:1–3; Isaiah 11:2; Isaiah 42:1; Isaiah 45:1; Luke 4:18–21; Acts 10:38

sections.h: Isaiah 65–66: new heavens and a new earth
sections.b: The phrase "new heavens and a new earth" comes from Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22. God says, "I am creating", with the verb of Genesis 1:1, and the next lines describe a Jerusalem of joy: no weeping, no infant deaths, long lives, houses lived in by those who build them, and peace among animals (Isaiah 65:18–25). The picture keeps ordinary life, transformed, and still includes death at a great age (Isaiah 65:20). 1 Enoch 91:16 and the Qumran texts take up the idea, and so does the New Testament: "we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness lives" (2 Peter 3:13), and "Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth" (Revelation 21:1). Readers differ on whether the new creation replaces the present world or renews it.
sections.refs: Isaiah 65:17–25; Isaiah 66:22; Genesis 1:1; 1 Enoch 91:16; 2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1–5; Romans 8:19–22

sections.h: Isaiah 60: the city of light
sections.b: Revelation's new Jerusalem draws more on Isaiah 60 than on any other chapter. Zion is told, "Rise up and shine, for your light has come" (Isaiah 60:1); nations walk toward her light, her gates stand open day and night so that the wealth of nations can be brought in (Isaiah 60:11), and "No longer will the sun be your light by day... the LORD will be your light forever" (Isaiah 60:19). Revelation 21:23–26 repeats these images: the city needs no sun or moon, "The nations will walk by its light", and "Its gates will never be shut by day". Isaiah 62 adds the city's new names, and Isaiah 65:18 says God is creating Jerusalem to be a joy. Revelation changes one thing: the city has no temple, for God and the Lamb are its temple (Revelation 21:22).
sections.refs: Isaiah 60:1–22; Isaiah 62:1–12; Isaiah 65:18–19; Revelation 21:2; Revelation 21:22–26; Revelation 22:5

sections.h: Isaiah 65:20: long life, and death still present
sections.b: Isaiah 65:20 promises that "whoever dies at a hundred will die young", in a passage that begins with new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17). Because death and sin are still mentioned, premillennial and dispensational readers take Isaiah 65:20–25 as a picture of Christ's thousand-year reign (Revelation 20:4–6), when the curse is lifted in part and people live long lives, before the final new creation. Amillennial readers answer that the prophet describes the eternal state in the language of this world, as a way of saying that life will be full. Postmillennial readers, such as Charles Hodge and Loraine Boettner, read it of a golden age of the gospel within history, before Christ returns. Early writers such as Justin and Irenaeus read the passage of an earthly kingdom in a rebuilt Jerusalem; Augustine read it of the age to come. See the traditions card on Isaiah 65.
sections.refs: Isaiah 65:17–25; Revelation 20:4–6; Revelation 21:4; Zechariah 8:4

sections.h: Isaiah 66:24: the undying worm
sections.b: The book of Isaiah ends with worshipers going out to look at "the corpses of the people who rebelled against me. For their worm will not die, and their fire will not be put out" (Isaiah 66:24). The scene is outside Jerusalem, and later readers placed it in the Valley of Hinnom, where Josiah had defiled the site of child sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31–33). In Mark 9:47–48 Jesus warns of being thrown into Gehenna, "where their worm does not die and the fire is not put out", quoting this verse. The Hebrew word for "horror" in the same verse, dera'on, appears elsewhere only in Daniel 12:2, of those who awake "to shame and everlasting abhorrence". Because the book ends so darkly, synagogues repeat Isaiah 66:23 after the last verse.
sections.refs: Isaiah 66:24; Isaiah 66:23; 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31–33; Mark 9:43–48; Daniel 12:2; Judith 16:17

sections.h: Isaiah 63:1–6: the warrior from Edom
sections.b: In Isaiah 63:1–6 a watchman sees a figure coming "from Edom, from Bozrah in clothes dyed red": the LORD, returning from treading the nations like grapes. The poem plays on the names: Edom sounds like 'adom, "red", and Bozrah like batsir, "grape harvest". Edom had joined in Jerusalem's fall (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 10–14), and Isaiah 34 had already pictured God's sword drenched in Edom's blood. In rabbinic writing Edom stood for Rome, and the passage was read of the final judgment on it. Revelation 19:13–15 takes the stained robe and the winepress for the rider called the Word of God.
sections.refs: Isaiah 63:1–6; Isaiah 34:5–8; Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 10–14; Revelation 19:13–15

sections.h: Isaiah 63: grieving his holy spirit
sections.b: The phrase "holy spirit" appears in the Hebrew Bible only in Isaiah 63:10–11 and Psalm 51:11. In the people's lament, God's holy spirit was among Israel in the exodus, "the Spirit of the LORD gave them rest" (Isaiah 63:14), but they "rebelled and grieved his holy spirit" (Isaiah 63:10), and God became their enemy. Ephesians 4:30 echoes the verse: do not grieve God's holy Spirit. Christian readers have seen in Isaiah 63:7–16 the Father, the angel of his presence and the holy spirit together, an early hint of the Trinity; Jewish readers take the spirit as God's own presence among his people. Isaiah 59:21 and 61:1 also tie the Spirit to God's words in the mouths of his people and his anointed.
sections.refs: Isaiah 63:10–14; Psalm 51:11; Isaiah 59:21; Isaiah 61:1; Ephesians 4:30; Nehemiah 9:20

sections.h: Isaiah 63–65: Father, Redeemer, the God of Amen
sections.b: The lament of Isaiah 63:7–64:12 calls God "our Father" twice: "For you are our Father. Abraham does not know us... 'Our Redeemer from Long Ago' is your name" (Isaiah 63:16), and "But now, LORD, you are our Father. We are the clay, and you are the one who shaped us" (Isaiah 64:8). God is rarely addressed as Father in the Hebrew Bible, and these verses shaped the Jewish prayer Avinu Malkenu, "Our Father, our King". Isaiah 65:16 gives another name found only there, "the God of Amen", the God whose word is firm; Revelation 3:14 calls Christ "the Amen". Isaiah 66:13 adds a mother's comfort: "so I myself will comfort you".
sections.refs: Isaiah 63:16; Isaiah 64:8; Isaiah 65:16; Isaiah 66:13; Deuteronomy 32:6; Malachi 2:10; Revelation 3:14

sections.h: Isaiah 62: Hephzibah and Beulah
sections.b: Isaiah 61:10 and 62:4–5 picture Zion's restoration as a wedding. The city once called "Abandoned" and "Desolate" will be called "My Delight Is in Her" (Hephzibah), and her land "Married" (Beulah), "For the LORD delights in you". "With a bridegroom's joy over his bride your God will rejoice over you" (Isaiah 62:5). The names were real women's names: Hephzibah was King Manasseh's mother (2 Kings 21:1). Through the KJV, Beulah became a name for heaven in hymns and in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress. The image continues into the New Testament's bride of Christ and the wedding of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7; Revelation 21:2).
sections.refs: Isaiah 61:10; Isaiah 62:1–5; Isaiah 54:5–6; 2 Kings 21:1; Revelation 19:7; Revelation 21:2

sections.h: Isaiah 59 and 62: no one to step in, and those who give God no rest
sections.b: Isaiah 59:16 says that God looked and "was shocked that no one stepped in", using mafgia', the word used of the servant who "will step in for the rebels" in Isaiah 53:12. So God acted himself. In Isaiah 62:6–7 the picture reverses: God posts guards on Jerusalem's walls who "all day and all night... will never keep silent", and tells those who keep the LORD reminded, "do not rest, and give him no rest" until he makes the city firm. The verse has been a charter for persistent prayer, like the widow who wears down the judge in Luke 18:1–8.
sections.refs: Isaiah 59:16; Isaiah 53:12; Isaiah 62:1; Isaiah 62:6–7; Isaiah 63:5; Luke 18:1–8

sections.h: Isaiah 59–63: God the redeemer who comes to Zion
sections.b: The go'el was the near relative who bought back land or freedom and avenged a death (Leviticus 25:25; Numbers 35:19). In Isaiah 40–66 God is Israel's go'el, and chapters 59–63 bring both sides of the role together. "A redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from rebellion" (Isaiah 59:20), words Paul quotes in Romans 11:26; the warrior from Edom says "the year to redeem my own had come", beside "a day of vengeance" (Isaiah 63:4); and the people pray, "'Our Redeemer from Long Ago' is your name" (Isaiah 63:16). The new names of Zion's people include "the Redeemed of the LORD" (Isaiah 62:12).
sections.refs: Isaiah 59:20; Isaiah 60:16; Isaiah 62:12; Isaiah 63:4; Isaiah 63:16; Leviticus 25:25; Numbers 35:19; Romans 11:26

sections.h: Isaiah 56 and 66: a house of prayer, and a house no one can build
sections.b: Isaiah 56–66 speaks of the temple in two directions. God promises foreigners joy "in my house of prayer", "for my house will be called a house of prayer for all the peoples" (Isaiah 56:7), and the nations bring offerings to beautify "the place of my sanctuary" (Isaiah 60:7, 13). But the book's last chapter begins: "The heavens are my throne, and the earth is the stool for my feet. Where then is the house that you would build for me?" (Isaiah 66:1), and God looks instead to "the poor one, stricken in spirit, who trembles at my word" (Isaiah 66:2). The lament in between mourns the burned temple (Isaiah 63:18; 64:11). Jesus quoted Isaiah 56:7 in the temple court (Mark 11:17), and Stephen quoted Isaiah 66:1–2 before the council (Acts 7:48–50).
sections.refs: Isaiah 56:7; Isaiah 60:7; Isaiah 60:13; Isaiah 64:11; Isaiah 66:1–2; Mark 11:17; Acts 7:48–50; 1 Kings 8:27

sections.h: Isaiah 63:7–64:12: a lament from the ruins
sections.b: Isaiah 63:7–64:12 is one of the longest community laments in the Bible. It begins by remembering "the LORD's acts of loyal love" in the exodus (Isaiah 63:7–14), turns to complaint ("Where are your zeal and your mighty deeds?", Isaiah 63:15), confesses sin ("like a cloth from a woman's monthly period are all our right deeds", Isaiah 64:6), appeals to God as Father and potter (Isaiah 64:8), and ends with a question: "Will you keep silent and crush us beyond all bounds?" (Isaiah 64:12). The temple lies burned (Isaiah 64:11), as in Lamentations and Psalms 74 and 79. In the book as it stands, God answers at once in chapter 65.
sections.refs: Isaiah 63:7–64:12; Isaiah 65:1; Psalm 74:1–11; Psalm 79:1–5; Lamentations 5:19–22

sections.h: Isaiah 56–66: what is written and what is read
sections.b: Several notes in Isaiah 56–66 turn on the difference between the written Hebrew (Ketiv) and the reading tradition (Qere). In Isaiah 63:9 the written text says "not" (lo') and the reading tradition "to him" (lo): either "in all their distress he did not afflict them" or "in all their distress, trouble came to him", the source of the teaching that God suffers with his people. In Isaiah 60:21 the written text has "his planting" and the reading "my planting"; in Isaiah 65:4, "pieces" or "broth"; in Isaiah 66:17, a masculine or feminine "one in the middle". In Isaiah 56:10 the written text reads "they have watched" and the reading tradition "its watchmen". The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran sometimes supports the written form (Isaiah 63:9) and sometimes the reading (Isaiah 65:4).
sections.refs: Isaiah 56:10; Isaiah 60:21; Isaiah 63:9; Isaiah 65:4; Isaiah 66:17
